name: mdy
comment: MDY is not Markdown, and this grammar no longer borrows Markdown's. It used to `include: text.html.markdown` and inject template tags into it, which needed an `injections` entry with priority to reach inside the contexts that grammar opens for headings, lists and emphasis. None of that is here any more: every MDY block rule is anchored to the start of its own line, so the whole language is a flat list of line patterns and there is nothing to inject into. The reference implementation is the demo editor's own highlighter (packages/mdy-site/src/syntax.js), which walks the source with the parser's own lexical rules; where this file cannot match it — a TextMate grammar sees one line at a time and cannot count brackets — the approximation is written down in the rule that makes it.

body.comment: Everything that is not front matter, in the order the parser takes it. Code first: the script stage runs over the whole document before any of the grammar does, so a `%` line is JavaScript wherever it is written, inside a fenced block included. Fences next, then comments, then the block rules, then inline.

frontmatter-start.comment: YAML front matter at the very start of the file. A TextMate grammar tokenizes one line at a time, so a begin pattern can never look ahead to confirm a later line is a bare +++ (the real, only rule src/mdy.js uses — see FRONT_MATTER_SEPARATOR/parseDocument). This approximates it from the one line we CAN see: front matter starts where the first line looks like a YAML `key:` mapping entry, or is +++ itself (an empty front-matter block, which parseDocument explicitly allows). A document whose body happens to open with `Word: text` is the one (rare) case this over-triggers on.
frontmatter-start.name: meta.frontmatter.mdy

document-separator.comment: A bare --- line splits a source into multiple documents (splitDocuments). Each new document may have its own front matter, checked the same heuristic way as frontmatter-start, against the line immediately following the separator; otherwise this --- is just a plain separator and what follows is body. `end` is a zero-width lookahead for any real (non-newline) character, deliberately NOT [\s\S]: vscode-textmate appends a synthetic trailing newline to every tokenized line (so $ anchors work), and [\s\S] would match THAT, closing this region one line too early — before the nested front-matter pattern below ever gets a look at the real next line. The separator carries markup.heading.* IN ADDITION to its punctuation scope (space-separated names push both onto the token's scope stack, deeper one last): a bare --- is the file's most structural line — it starts a whole new document — and plain punctuation scopes render dim in most themes. Same treatment for the +++ front-matter fences.
document-separator.name: meta.after-document-separator.mdy

script-block.comment: `%%` says that what follows it is more code, and runs on into the lines under it as far as the line that brings its brackets back to even (see scriptLines in src/parse/script.js). Brackets are exactly what a TextMate grammar cannot count, so this approximates the extent the way these blocks are actually written: it ends after the first line whose own first character is a closing bracket, and before any line that starts a new `%` of its own. An unusual block ends late and paints a line or two of markup as JavaScript; it can never swallow the rest of the file, because a later `%` line always closes it.
script-block.name: meta.embedded.block.mdy

script-line.comment: One `%` line is one line of code. What it leaves open encloses the markup under it — which is how a loop is written — so its brackets are deliberately not counted and the region is exactly this line. Leading space carries no meaning: the parser lifts a `%` line out before it counts a single column, so how far in the author writes their code is their own business. `\%` at the start of a line is the literal character instead, handled by #escape and matched one column earlier, so it wins.
script-line.name: meta.embedded.line.mdy

fence.comment: Three or more backticks or tildes fence a block of code. Everything up to the closing fence is content, whatever it looks like — the first word after the opener names the language. \1 makes the closer match the opener's own run, so a longer fence holds a shorter one and a tilde fence holds backticks.
fence.name: markup.fenced_code.block.mdy

comment-line.comment: A `#` with whitespace after it, or alone on its line, is a comment: it comes off after the code has run and before anything is parsed, so it never reaches the tree. `#tag` has no space and is a reference instead.
comment-line.name: comment.line.number-sign.mdy

heading.comment: A line starting with `=` is a heading, the number of `=` being the level. Trailing `=` are decoration.
heading.name: markup.heading.mdy

underline.comment: A line of only `=`, or of four or more `-`, under a paragraph underlines it Setext style. Three dashes are the document separator and are matched earlier; one is a list item and two are an em dash, which is why an underline starts at four.
underline.name: markup.heading.underline.mdy

thematic-break.comment: Three or more `-`, `*` or `_` alone on a line, spaces between them allowed. Exactly `---` never reaches here: that spelling belongs to the document separator.
thematic-break.name: punctuation.definition.thematic-break.mdy markup.heading.break.mdy

element.comment: A line starting with `<` opens an element, and everything indented two columns past it is its content — there is no closing tag to match, so this is a single-line rule and the nesting is the indentation's business, not the grammar's. Space after the `<` means nothing, the closing `>` is optional, and anything after it is inline content.

list-item.comment: Markdown's lists, unchanged: `-`, `*` or `+` for bullets, `1.` or `1)` for numbers, and the marker has to be followed by whitespace so `---` and `-5` stay prose. A `[ ]` or `[x]` straight after the marker makes the item a task.

table-row.comment: GitHub's tables, unchanged. A delimiter row (`| :--- | ---: |`) is scoped apart from a content row, because it is the row that says what the table is.

escape.comment: A backslash before `{{` opts a line out of interpolation, and a backslash before the `%` a line opens with does the same for a code line — both come off in the output. Listed before every rule they could collide with; at the same position it is not even needed, since the escape's match starts one column earlier and leftmost always wins.
escape.name: constant.character.escape.mdy

interpolation.comment: `{{ expr }}` in content is a JavaScript expression interpolated into the line. It closes at the FIRST `}}`, matching the compiler (which uses indexOf, not brace counting). contentName, NOT name: meta.embedded.line.mdy is mapped to JavaScript in package.json's embeddedLanguages, and a region's `name` covers its begin/end delimiters too — which made VSCode treat the braces themselves as JS-language brackets and rainbow-colorize them as nested pairs.
interpolation.name: meta.template.expression.mdy

code-span.comment: A double backtick opens a raw span: nothing inside it is markup until the next one.
code-span.name: markup.inline.raw.mdy

wiki-link.comment: `[[ label ]]` or `[[ label | /where ]]`. Without a `|` the label is slugified into the URL, which is the same slugifier a heading's id comes from.
wiki-link.name: meta.link.wiki.mdy

autolink.comment: URLs in text become links, found before markers so the `//` in `https://` never opens a run of emphasis. Bare domains are not links — a two-letter country code is a valid suffix, so matching those would turn README.md and node.js into links.
autolink.name: markup.underline.link.mdy

reference.comment: `#tag` and `@user`, each only at the start of a word — which is what keeps the `#` of a URL fragment and the `@` of an email address out of it. The name starts with a letter or an underscore, never a digit, so `#42` stays the issue number it was written as.
reference.name: variable.other.reference.mdy

marker.comment: Inline formatting toggles rather than nesting: the first occurrence of a sequence opens the span and the next occurrence of the same sequence closes it. A TextMate grammar has no way to model a toggle, so each sequence is scoped where it appears and the theme colours the marker itself — the same information, without pretending to a structure the language does not have.

js-in-interpolation.comment: JS highlighting inside `{{ }}`. Strings and comments are guarded against `}}` — the compiler closes at the first one even inside a string (indexOf knows no JS), so a construct that spanned the closer would both diverge from the compiler and eat the delimiter. Guarded constructs simply stop highlighting at the closer; the plain text that remains is a smaller loss than a swallowed delimiter.

js.comment: JS highlighting on a `%` or `%%` line. Nothing is guarded here: a code line runs to the end of the line and a `%%` block to the line that closes it, so there is no delimiter further along for a string or a comment to eat.

js-common.comment: Region-free JS token rules shared by every code context. `$` before a `.` is the document's native-function namespace ($.find, $.render, $.emit, $.resize, …) — highlighted like a language-provided variable, not a plain identifier; `req`, `res` and `transform` are the three names a document is always handed.

typography.comment: The three substitutions the parser makes inside text (docs/language.md, Typography): three dots become an ellipsis, exactly two dashes become an em dash, and the drawn arrows become their characters. Each is written exactly, never as a run — '....' is four dots and '--->' is a rule, not a longer arrow — so every pattern is bounded on both sides. Arrows come first because '<-->' and '==>' both contain sequences the em-dash rule would otherwise take a bite out of.

patterns.name: constant.character.dash.mdy
patterns.comment: Exactly two: a longer run is a thematic break or a rule.

patterns.name: constant.character.ellipsis.mdy
patterns.comment: Exactly three, for the same reason.
